Heardest
HERD-est
v. (2nd pers. sing., past t.)
The second-person singular past of hear, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it as the form used with thou. Scripture uses it in both directions: of God hearing a man’s cry, and of a man having heard God’s word and being answerable for it.

Biblical Definition

Heardest runs both ways in Scripture, and both are consoling in their own manner. Godward it is the language of answered prayer: For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee (Psalm 31:22). The psalmist confesses that his despairing conclusion was simply wrong; he was never cut off, and the hearing was going on while he believed it was not. Nehemiah’s national confession rehearses the same mercy at the beginning of the nation’s history: And didst see the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heardest their cry by the Red sea (Nehemiah 9:9). Manward, the word measures responsibility. God commends Josiah for what happened in him when the recovered book was read: Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD, when thou heardest what I spake against this place… and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the LORD (2 Kings 22:19) — and the last clause turns the word back Godward, hearing answered by hearing. Caleb appeals to what Joshua had heard forty-five years earlier and asks for the hardest ground in Canaan on the strength of it: thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there, and that the cities were great and fenced (Joshua 14:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives HEARDEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb hear, used with thou: didst perceive by the ear; didst listen to; didst attend to; and, of God, didst regard and answer, as prayer.

expand to see more

HEARDEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb HEAR; used with the pronoun thou.

HEAR, v.t. — To perceive by the ear; to feel an impression of sound by the proper organs.

To give audience or allowance to speak; to listen to; to attend to.

To regard; to attend to with favour; and hence, of God, to answer — as, the LORD heard my supplication.

From Saxon hyran, to hear — the root also of hearken, hearing, and the older hearsay.

Key Scripture

Psalm 31:22 — "For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee."

Nehemiah 9:9 — "And didst see the affliction of our fathers in Egypt, and heardest their cry by the Red sea;"

2 Kings 22:19 — "Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD, when thou heardest what I spake against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the LORD."

Joshua 14:12 — "Now therefore give me this mountain, whereof the LORD spake in that day; for thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there, and that the cities were great and fenced: if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out, as the LORD said."

Modern Corruption

Josiah’s response to hearing the Word — a tender heart, humbling, rent clothes and weeping — is the reaction Scripture commends, and the modern habit of hearing preaching as content consumed rather than as God speaking has largely retired it.

expand to see more

The book found in the temple had been lost long enough that a reigning king did not know what was in it, and when it was read he tore his clothes. God’s commendation in 2 Kings 22:19 lists four things in order: a tender heart, self-humbling, torn clothes, and weeping — and then adds I also have heard thee. That is the biblical shape of hearing the Word: it produces grief, and the grief is itself heard. Set against it, the ordinary modern posture toward preaching is evaluative — the sermon is judged for interest, usefulness, or delivery, and the hearer leaves with an opinion rather than a wound. A congregation may be highly informed and never once tender, and Josiah’s reformation began at the point where the two diverge.

Psalm 31:22 addresses the opposite failure, which is a real one and not to be scolded away. The psalmist said in his haste that he was cut off from God’s eyes, and he was mistaken; the hearing was happening the whole time. Scripture is unembarrassed to record a saint’s despairing verdict on his own case and then correct it, which is why the psalms remain the church’s book for the worst weeks. Note the order: he does not first feel heard and then believe it. He learns afterward that he was heard, and writes the psalm so that the next sufferer may know it earlier. Joshua 14:12 shows a third use — Caleb asking for the hill country of the giants precisely because Joshua had heard the report and knew what it cost.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shama (H8085), to hear, to listen, to obey; azan (H238), to give ear; Greek akouo (G191), to hear; eisakouo (G1522), to hear favourably, to answer.

expand to see more

Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, and by extension to obey; the first word of the Shema, Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4).

Hebrew azan (H238) — to give ear, to listen closely; formed from ozen, the ear.

Greek akouo (G191) — to hear; faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17).

Greek eisakouo (G1522) — to hear so as to answer; used of God answering prayer (Matthew 6:7; Hebrews 5:7).

Greek hupakouo (G5219) — to hear under, to obey; the New Testament word for obedience is a hearing word.

Usage

"Thou heardest the voice of my supplications (Psalm 31:22) — the hearing was going on while he believed it was not."

"When thou heardest what I spake against this place (2 Kings 22:19) — the commended reaction to the Word: tenderness, humbling, grief."

"Thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there (Joshua 14:12) — Caleb asking for the hardest ground on the strength of what was heard."
